chapters.title: Patterns in Mathematics
chapters.objectives: Recognise and explain number patterns; connect dot arrangements with triangular and square numbers.
chapters.revision: Write several terms before guessing a rule. Consecutive square numbers differ by successive odd numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16 have gaps 3, 5, 7. Triangular numbers count rows of 1, 2, 3, ... dots. A pattern rule should explain every given term; a short list alone need not determine a unique continuation.

questions.text: Using the rule “add the next odd number”, continue 1, 4, 9, 16 by two terms.
steps: The differences so far are 3, 5 and 7.
Add 9 to 16 to get 25.
Add 11 to 25 to get 36. These are the next two square numbers.

questions.text: A dot triangle has rows containing 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 dots. How many dots does it contain?
steps: Count each row once.
The three pairs each total 7, so there are 3 × 7 = 21 dots.

questions.text: Starting at 7, double the previous term each time. Write the next three terms and explain the rule.
steps: 28 × 2 = 56. The rule multiplies the previous term by 2; it does not add a fixed number.

chapters.title: Lines and Angles
chapters.objectives: Distinguish a line, ray and line segment; measure, compare and classify angles.
chapters.revision: A line extends endlessly in both directions. A ray has one endpoint; a line segment has two. An angle measures the opening between two rays with a common endpoint. Acute angles are smaller than 90°, a right angle is 90°, obtuse angles lie between 90° and 180°, and a straight angle is 180°. Use the protractor scale that begins at zero on the starting arm.

questions.text: Classify angles of 38°, 90°, 127° and 180°.
steps: 38° is greater than 0° and less than 90°, so it is acute.
90° is a right angle.
127° is between 90° and 180°, so it is obtuse. 180° is a straight angle.

questions.text: Two adjoining angles make a straight angle. One measures 64°. Find the other.
steps: A straight angle measures 180°.
Subtract the known part: 180° − 64° = 116°.

questions.text: Draw a ray AB. Use a protractor to construct an angle of 52° at A. Describe the steps.
steps: Place the protractor centre on A and align its zero line with ray AB.
On the scale beginning at zero along AB, mark point C at 52°.
Draw ray AC. Check that the opening from AB to AC is 52°; the drawing is acute.

chapters.title: Number Play
chapters.objectives: Explore digit operations, palindromes and estimation; explain each operation rather than assuming a pattern always holds.
chapters.revision: A digit sum adds the digits of a number. A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. Reverse-and-add is an exploration, not a promise that every starting number quickly becomes a palindrome. When estimating, state what you rounded and use the estimate to judge whether an exact result is reasonable.

questions.text: Find the digit sum of 5836. Is 5836 a palindrome?
steps: Add the digits: 5 + 8 + 3 + 6 = 22.
The reversed digits give 6385.
Since 5836 and 6385 are different, 5836 is not a palindrome.

questions.text: Apply reverse-and-add once to 47. Is the result a palindrome?
steps: Reverse 47 to get 74.
121 reads identically in either direction. This verifies this example only.

questions.text: Estimate 392 + 608 by rounding each number to the nearest hundred, then calculate the exact total.
steps: 392 rounds to 400 and 608 rounds to 600.
The estimated total is 400 + 600 = 1000.
The exact total is 392 + 608 = 1000, which agrees with the estimate.

chapters.title: Data Handling and Presentation
chapters.objectives: Organise categorical data, interpret a key and read a bar graph with a stated scale.
chapters.revision: A frequency is the number of times a category occurs. Give a table or graph a title and label its categories and scale. In a pictograph, the key tells how many objects one symbol represents. A bar graph uses separated bars for categories; read heights from the scale rather than comparing appearances alone.

questions.text: A class votes for a game: chess 7 votes, badminton 9, kho-kho 6. Find the total and the most popular game.
steps: Add the frequencies: 7 + 9 + 6 = 22.
Compare 7, 9 and 6. The largest is 9.
Badminton has 9 votes, so it is the most popular of these choices.

questions.text: In a pictograph, one complete star represents 4 books. A shelf has 7 complete stars. How many books are shown?
steps: Read the key: 1 star means 4 books.
There are 7 stars, so multiply 7 × 4.
The shelf is represented by 28 books.

questions.text: A bar graph uses 1 vertical division for 3 plants. The Monday bar is 5 divisions high and the Tuesday bar is 8 divisions high. How many more plants were counted on Tuesday?
steps: Monday represents 5 × 3 = 15 plants.
Tuesday represents 8 × 3 = 24 plants.
24 − 15 = 9 more plants were counted on Tuesday.

chapters.title: Prime Time
chapters.objectives: Find factors and multiples, distinguish primes and composites, and use prime factorisation and divisibility tests.
chapters.revision: A factor divides a number exactly; a multiple is obtained by multiplying by a whole number. A prime number has exactly two positive factors, 1 and itself. The number 1 is neither prime nor composite. Co-prime numbers have no common positive factor other than 1; they need not both be prime. Prime factorisation writes a number as a product of primes.

questions.text: Write the prime factorisation of 84.
steps: Therefore 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7. All four factors are prime.

questions.text: Are 14 and 25 co-prime? Justify using their factors.
steps: The positive factors of 14 are 1, 2, 7 and 14.
The positive factors of 25 are 1, 5 and 25.
Their only common factor is 1, so they are co-prime, although both are composite.

questions.text: Is 438 divisible by 2, 3 and 9? Explain each decision.
steps: The last digit is 8, so 438 is divisible by 2.
The digit sum is 4 + 3 + 8 = 15. Since 15 is divisible by 3, so is 438.
15 is not divisible by 9, so 438 is not divisible by 9.

chapters.title: Perimeter and Area
chapters.objectives: Distinguish boundary length and surface covered; calculate rectangle and square measures with correct units.
chapters.revision: Perimeter measures the total boundary length and uses units such as cm. Area measures the surface covered and uses square units such as cm². For a rectangle of length l and width w, perimeter = 2(l + w) and area = l × w. For a square of side s, perimeter = 4s and area = s². Equal areas do not force equal perimeters.

questions.text: A rectangular card measures 11 cm by 7 cm. Find its perimeter and area.
steps: Area = 11 × 7 = 77 cm².
The perimeter is a length; the area is measured in square centimetres.

questions.text: A square has perimeter 28 cm. Find its side length and area.
steps: A square has four equal sides.
Each side is 28 ÷ 4 = 7 cm.
Area = 7 × 7 = 49 cm².

questions.text: Rectangles A and B measure 9 cm by 4 cm and 12 cm by 3 cm. Compare their areas and perimeters.
questions.answer: Both areas 36 cm²; perimeters 26 cm and 30 cm
steps: Area of A = 9 × 4 = 36 cm²; area of B = 12 × 3 = 36 cm².
Perimeter of A = 2 × (9 + 4) = 26 cm.
Perimeter of B = 2 × (12 + 3) = 30 cm. Equal areas can have different perimeters.

chapters.title: Fractions
chapters.objectives: Interpret equal shares and number-line positions; compare and add fractions using equivalent units.
chapters.revision: A fraction counts equal-sized parts of a whole. Equivalent fractions name the same quantity: multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number preserves the value. To compare or add fractions, express them with a common denominator. Never add denominators when adding fractions with the same denominator.

questions.text: Calculate 5/12 + 1/6 in simplest form.
steps: Use denominator 12: 1/6 = 2/12.
7 and 12 have no common factor greater than 1, so 7/12 is simplest.

questions.text: Which is greater, 7/10 or 2/3? Show a common-denominator comparison.
steps: A common denominator of 10 and 3 is 30.
21/30 is greater than 20/30, so 7/10 is greater.

questions.text: A 3-metre ribbon is shared equally among 4 children. How much ribbon does each receive?
steps: Equal sharing means dividing the total by 4.
3 ÷ 4 = 3/4 metre per child.
Check: four shares of 3/4 metre make 12/4 = 3 metres.

chapters.title: Playing with Constructions
chapters.objectives: Use a ruler, compass and perpendicular lines to construct and check squares and rectangles.
chapters.revision: A construction must meet its stated measurements, not merely look right. A rectangle has four right angles and opposite sides equal. A square also has all four sides equal. Keep a compass opening fixed while transferring a length. Check perpendicular sides and the final lengths; rectangle diagonals are equal, but equality of diagonals alone does not prove any quadrilateral is a rectangle.

questions.text: Describe how to construct a square ABCD of side 4.5 cm using a ruler and set square.
questions.answer: Four 4.5 cm sides and four right angles
steps: Draw AB = 4.5 cm. At A and B, draw perpendicular rays on the same side of AB.
Mark AD = 4.5 cm and BC = 4.5 cm on these rays. Join C to D.
Check CD = 4.5 cm and all four angles are right angles. The construction gives square ABCD in order.

questions.text: A student draws a rectangle 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. What lengths must its opposite sides have, and how should each corner be checked?
questions.answer: Opposite lengths 8 cm and 5 cm; each corner 90°
steps: Opposite sides of a rectangle have equal lengths.
The side opposite the 8 cm side must be 8 cm; the side opposite the 5 cm side must be 5 cm.
Use a set square or protractor to check all four corners are 90°. Equal opposite sides alone are insufficient.

questions.text: The diagonals AC and BD of a constructed rectangle are measured. AC is 9.2 cm. What should BD measure, allowing for drawing accuracy?
steps: A rectangle has equal diagonals.
AC and BD join opposite vertices.
Therefore BD should also measure 9.2 cm, within the precision of the drawing and ruler.

chapters.title: Symmetry
chapters.objectives: Identify reflection axes and rotational symmetry, including the smallest angle of turn.
chapters.revision: A line of symmetry divides a figure so that reflection across the line maps the whole figure onto itself. Rotational symmetry means a turn smaller than a full turn maps the figure onto itself. The rotational order counts matches during one full 360° turn, including the final position. For an order n figure, the smallest angle of turn is 360° ÷ n.

questions.text: For an unmarked square, state the number of lines of symmetry and the smallest angle of rotational symmetry.
steps: Two symmetry axes pass through the midpoints of opposite sides. Two more follow the diagonals.
This gives 4 lines of reflection symmetry.
A quarter turn maps the square onto itself, so the smallest turn is 360° ÷ 4 = 90°.

questions.text: An unmarked rectangle is 10 cm by 6 cm. How many reflection axes does it have? Does a 90° turn map it onto itself?
steps: One axis passes through the midpoints of the two long sides; another passes through the midpoints of the two short sides.
Its diagonals are not reflection axes because the adjacent side lengths differ.
A 90° turn exchanges the 10 cm and 6 cm directions, so the rectangle does not match. A 180° turn does match.

questions.text: A figure has rotational symmetry of order 6. Find its smallest positive angle of rotation.
steps: A full turn is 360°.
Order 6 means six equally spaced matching positions in that turn.
The smallest angle is 360° ÷ 6 = 60°.

chapters.title: The Other Side of Zero
chapters.objectives: Represent signed quantities on a number line; compare integers and interpret addition and subtraction.
chapters.revision: Integers extend the number line to include negative whole numbers. Moving right increases the number; moving left decreases it. Zero separates positive and negative numbers and is neither positive nor negative. Opposite integers such as 5 and −5 sum to zero. Use signed quantities consistently when representing temperatures, floors, gains or losses.

questions.text: At dawn the temperature is −4°C. It rises by 9°C. Find the new temperature.
steps: Start at −4 on the number line.
A rise of 9 moves nine units to the right: −4 + 9.
Four units reach zero; five more reach 5. The temperature is 5°C.

questions.text: Arrange −8, 3, 0, −2 and 5 in increasing order.
steps: Increasing order goes from left to right on a number line.
Among these negatives, −8 is left of −2. Both are less than zero.
The positive numbers follow zero, with 3 before 5.

questions.text: A lift starts on floor +3 and goes down 7 floors. At which numbered floor does it stop? Count floor 0 as a floor.
steps: Going down is a negative change, so calculate 3 − 7.
Three floors down reaches 0. Four further floors down reaches −4.
The lift stops at floor −4.
